paper_title: Read, Allocate, Route: Role-Coupled Tokenization for Pixel-Space Generative Transformers

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Pixel-space generative Transformers typically use one token per image patch, so capturing finer detail requires more tokens and makes global attention increasingly expensive. We observe that finer detail does not necessarily require more global communication: low-frequency structure benefits from global exchange, while high-frequency detail can be modeled locally. Based on this insight, we introduce SpecSlot, a pixel-space rectified-flow Transformer that decouples output detail from the length of the global attention sequence. SpecSlot expands each spatial anchor into multiple slots, each assigned a disjoint band of DCT coefficients; this separates anchor density from spectral subdivision. Only the lowest-frequency slot from each anchor participates in global attention, while all slots interact locally. This allows the model to increase spectral detail without enlarging the global sequence. A spatial head further adds a local correction to the spectral prediction, while the generative state, target, and loss remain in pixel space. On ImageNet-256, SpecSlot achieves a comparable final FID to a FLOPs-matched JiT control while converging faster. On ImageNet-512, it improves FID by 2.84 over the control with 3.9% fewer FLOPs, and comes within only 0.69 FID of JiT-B/16 at 38.2% lower cost. On text-to-image generation, SpecSlot surpasses JiT-B/8 on DPG-Bench by 1.06 at 40.6% lower forward cost.

sections.title: 1 Introduction
sections.content: Pixel-space generative models learn directly from noise to pixels, eliminating the separately trained autoencoder and its compression bottleneck. This simplicity, however, comes with computational cost: the full-resolution image must be represented as Transformer tokens. Most pixel-space Transformers use one token per spatial patch, so the patch grid simultaneously determines what the model reads, what each token predicts, and how many tokens participate in global attention. As result, finer image detail directly increases attention cost: on 256 256 image, reducing the patch size from 16 16 to 8 8 increases the token count from 256 to 1,024, making the quadratic term of dense attention 16 larger. 1 Figure 2 SpecSlot data flow. Each anchor expands into slots. blocks process lowest-radial slot-0 carriers across anchors with context states; blocks mix all slots within each anchor. The final slot states decode lapped-DCT spectral base and an anchor-aligned spatial correction, summed in pixel space. Existing methods address this cost from different directions, but largely retain the coupling between output detail and token communication. JiT routes every patch token through the global sequence [1]. Multiscale systems move detail to extra stages or detailer heads [2, 3, 4], and efficient-attention methods shorten the sequence with generic patternswindows, selected global tokens, or learned sparsity [5, 6, 7, 8]. Spectral Forcing brings in frequency structure, but only to filter the noisy input; its tokens remain spatial patches [9]. Across the pixel-space generators discussed above, output detail remains tied to spatial patch grid, even when communication is compressed or restricted. Our key observation is that finer detail does not necessarily require proportionally more global communication: in the frequency domain, low-frequency structure carries broad image organization and benefits from long-range exchange, while fine detail is largely local. token carrying broad structure therefore stands to gain from exchanging with the whole image, while token carrying fine detail mostly does not. Yet in existing designs, what token communicates is fixed by where it sits, not by what it produces. Can tokens output role also determine how it should communicate? SpecSlot builds on this idea by making output roles explicit and using them to control communication. It organizes computation around three operations: Read, Allocate, and Route. Read forms grid of spatial anchors that collect input evidence. Allocate expands each anchor into indexed slots, with each slot assigned disjoint radial group of DCT coefficients. Route then uses these spectral roles to decide communication: only the slot assigned the lowest-frequency group from each anchor enters the global stage, while all slots interact locally within the anchor. This separates fine-grained output representation from the length of the global sequence. spatial head further reuses the same slot states to add local correction to the spectral prediction, without introducing additional tokens. Figure 2 illustrates this design. This representation exposes two separate allocation variables. controls the density of spatial anchors, while controls the spectral subdivision at each anchor. The total number of slots grows with K, but the global image sequence contains only carriers. fixed token budget can therefore be allocated either to denser spatial anchors or to finer spectral roles without forcing both to increase together. This turns tokenization from single patch-size choice into an explicit qualitycompute allocation problem. Our contributions are: We introduce an indexed representation in which spatial anchors collect input evidence and slots receive disjoint spectral coefficient groups. The split exposes anchor density and coefficient subdivision as separate allocation variables, and the same slot states also decode local pixel correction. We define carrier-routed globalgloballocallocal (GGLL) attention from the slot index: one lowest-radial carrier per anchor enters global blocks, and all slots enter anchor-local blocks, so the global sequence contains carriers rather than slots. On ImageNet-256 and ImageNet-512, SpecSlot provides two measured qualitycompute operating points between JiTs low-cost and high-cost settings. At ImageNet-512, W256/K4 lowers FID by 2.84 over our FLOPs-matched JiT control (JiT-CM) with 3.9% fewer GFLOPs, and trails JiT-B/16 by 0.69 FID at 38.2% lower cost. Larger output windows cover more pixels while the global sequence remains fixed; the larger improvement over JiT-CM is consistent with this within-anchor allocation. On text-to-image generation, SpecSlot likewise surpasses JiT-B/8 on DPG-Bench by 1.06 at 40.6% lower forward cost.

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: Diffusion and pixel-space generation. Diffusion and score-based models learn to reverse gradual noising process and provide the iterative foundation of modern image synthesis [10, 11, 12]. Rectified flow turns the same idea into straight noise-to-data path [13]. Latent diffusion moved this process into the latent space of separately trained autoencoder, and improved autoencoders continue to strengthen this line [14, 15, 16]. DiT, U-ViT, and SiT showed that plain Transformers scale reliably in this setting [17, 18, 19]. Pixel-space generation removes the autoencoder, but then asks the model to process the full-resolution state. This line has followed several routes: Simple Diffusion and Hourglass DiT reduce the state internally, cascaded models and PixelFlow distribute generation across resolutions, and JiT shows that direct large-patch Transformer can remain strong pixel-space baseline [1, 20, 21, 22, 23]. Detail recovery is then assigned to extra components: PixelDiT adds pixel-level DiT, DiP adds detailer head, HyperDiT connects coarse and fine flows, and PixNerd decodes patch tokens with neural field [2, 3, 4, 24]. These designs differ in where the compute goes, but share one premise: token is spatial patch, so finer detail and wider communication stay tied to the same spatial grid. SpecSlot complements this line with single-backbone allocation: indexed slots carry fixed output and communication roles, so detail can be subdivided without making every output token global. Frequency structure and transform-domain generation. Frequency offers complementary view of this problem. It has entered generative modeling through the state or forward process, through generation order or conditioning, and through the training objective or analysis. In the first line, inverse heat dissipation, wavelet models, sparse transform codes, and DCTdiff change the representation or process used for generation [25, 26, 27, 28, 29]. In the second, VAR and NFIG organize generation by scale or frequency, while Spectral Forcing and Frequency-Forcing use frequency-related conditioning or guidance; Latent Forcing instead reorders the trajectory with semantic auxiliary stream [9, 30, 31, 32, 33]. Focal frequency loss reweights spectral errors, and Fourier-space analyses characterize diffusion without changing the denoiser [34, 35]. Recent architectural methods make frequency roles part of the denoiser itself: DiMSUM alternates spatial and wavelet-subband processing, while DeCo assigns low and high frequencies to DiT and separate pixel decoder [36, 37]. Together these works show several ways for frequency to shape representation or generation, but the cited lines do not use fixed spectral groups as both per-token output ownership and communication eligibility within one pixel-space backbone. SpecSlot keeps the state, target, and loss in pixel space; fixed, disjoint DCT groups give slots spectral roles, and the role index also determines which slots communicate globally. Visual tokenization and allocation. Vision Transformers tokenize an image into spatial patch grid [38], and NaViT extends this idea to variable resolutions [39]. This line reduces sequence work by changing how many spatial tokens are retained or processed at each step: ToMe merges similar tokens, SparseDiT prunes them, DyDiT++ reschedules computation across denoising time and space, variable-length tokenization learns global merge, and FlexiDiT spends fewer tokens at easier steps [40, 41, 42, 43, 44]. The spatial patch remains the allocation unit, so detail and communication stay coupled to the same grid. SpecSlot adds second, spectral axis: each of anchors owns slots with disjoint coefficient groups, making the fixed budget =W an explicit split between anchor density and spectral subdivision. Global-local and sparse communication. The communication literature provides the other half of the problem by restricting how tokens exchange information. Swin uses local windows with shifted boundaries, Longformer combines local windows with few global tokens, and Perceiver routes information through small latent bottleneck [5, 6, 7]. In pixel-space generation, RINs exchange information through learned interface states, while trainable sparse attention and PixSGR learn or select interaction patterns from the data [8, 45, 46]. These approaches provide useful local or global topologies, but do not tie communication eligibility to fixed spectral output role. SpecSlot fixes the graph from the allocation: one lowest-frequency slot per anchor is the global carrier, and all slots interact locally, so cross-anchor communication is spent on the role that also carries the low-frequency scaffold. 3 Figure 3 SpecSlot allocation. patch grid spends all tokens in one global sequence; splitting =W into spatial anchors and spectral slots keeps global attention at carriers.

sections.title: 3 Methodology
sections.content: SpecSlot organizes pixel-space generation around one idea: tokenization as allocationassigning each token fixed output role and dividing fixed token budget between anchor density and spectral subdivision. Global attention is then spent only on the role that needs it; the rectified-flow state, target, and loss remain in pixel space.

sections.title: 3.2 SpecSlot Architecture
sections.content: Why is allocation needed? In patch-grid model, adding finer detail means shrinking the patch, and the global sequence grows with it; the two cannot be adjusted separately. Prior designs keep the spatial patch as the only allocation unit. SpecSlot instead introduces the missing variables, forming spatial anchors and expanding each anchor into indexed slots (Figure 3): = K, = 2s, = (H/s)2, = L2 = 4H 2 . (4) The budget splits into anchors that read the input and slots per anchor that divide the output; each slot owns an equal share of the coefficients per channel, with the input cell side and the output window side. The two variables act separately: sets how densely the input is read, and how finely the output is divided. At fixed , anchor density trades directly against spectral subdivision, and output detail can grow with while the global sequence stays at carriers. Equal does not imply equal cost, since communication and projection scale differently with the split. Three operations implement this allocation, as shown in Figure 2: Read collects each anchors input evidence, Allocate assigns each slot fixed output role, and Route lets the role decide communication. 3.2.1 Read: Spatial Anchors and Slot Expansion The first question is where input evidence comes from; SpecSlot reads it on grid of anchors, independent of how the output is divided. sections.title: 4.2 ImageNet Results
sections.content: On ImageNet-256, SpecSlot-K2 and SpecSlot-K4 are two measured, nondominated operating points between JiT-B/16 and JiT-B/8  (Table 1)  : K2 already improves over JiT-B/16, and K4 improves further while using 40.9% fewer FLOPs than JiT-B/8, which remains the quality leader. JiT-CM gives the closer compute comparison: SpecSlot-K4 matches its mean FID within the five-seed 95% interval at nearly identical FLOPs and throughput (Appendix D), and descends faster at early-to-mid checkpoints (Figure 4). At ImageNet-512, each anchor covers four times as many pixels as at ImageNet-256, while our global sequence stays at 288 tokens. Larger spectral windows and the spatial correction can accommodate the additional within-anchor detail without adding global communication, offering possible explanation for SpecSlots 7 Figure 5 Paired ImageNet-256 generations with the same class label and noise draw: SpecSlot W256/K4 and JiT-CM. sections.title: 4.3 Text-to-Image Generation
sections.content: Protocol. We test whether the allocation and routing design transfers from class labels to text conditions. We train at 256 256 on mixture of the BLIP3o long-caption and short-caption shards [53] and JourneyDB shards [54]. frozen OpenCLIP ViT-L/14 encoder [55] and trainable 32-query adapter provide the denoiser context. SpecSlot reads this context through its carrier states during the global route, while local blocks continue to process image slots; JiT uses the same text encoder and adapter. We retain the ImageNet rectifiedflow objective, optimizer, and EMA; the complete training contract is in Appendix Table 9. Evaluation uses the 50-step Heun sampler with CFG 4.0 for SpecSlot and 2.9 for JiT. Table 2 reports the results. Results. sections.title: 5.1 Understanding the Design
sections.content: 5.1.1 Anchor Density and Coefficient Subdivision Both allocation axes trade compute for quality, but they are not interchangeable: improves the read, refines the write  (Table 4)  . Increasing at fixed lowers FID at higher cost with diminishing returnsthe last doubling buys only 0.31 FIDwhile shifting the split toward more anchors at fixed lowers FID monotonically, with no clear saturation in this range. Within the tested =2,048 configurations, these trends favor allocating more of the token budget to spatial anchors; we do not claim that this rule generalizes beyond the measured range. At fixed and B, the entropy-effective slot fraction decreases monotonically from 0.803 at K=2 to 0.495 at K=8  (Table 5)  . The absolute effective rank still grows, but sublinearly, so token count alone does not measure effective capacity. Section 6.1 localizes this complementarity over the flow and across frequency bands. 5.1.3 Carrier Routing To test routing at fixed forward budget, we train full-global control (Dense-global-CM) on the same 256/K4 configuration, replacing the carrier/local schedule with 12 full-global blocks over all 1,024 image slots; its hidden width is 560, matching the measured GGLL forward cost. GGLL is both better and faster than this control at essentially identical FLOPs  (Table 3)  . Full-global attention reaches lower FID but at 74.8% higher cost and lower throughput. The carrier design therefore targets the intermediate, attention-constrained regime, saving 42.8% of the full-global cost. GLGL keeps the same carrier set and global budget but alternates the global/local order; its FID degrades at identical compute, showing that block order affects performance under this fixed carrier set. Section 6.2 provides possible motivation for early global processing: the lowest-radial role is recovered earliest in the flow.

sections.title: 6.1 Spectral Base and Spatial Correction
sections.content: Figure 7 shows the spectral term has the larger self-energy, while the spatial terms share grows from 0.07 to 0.23 over the flow, and the normalized cross term stays positivethe two terms reinforce, not cancel. Projected through the matched lapped-DCT analysis frame (which does not confer radial coefficient ownership), the spatial terms share is smallest in the lowest radial group and dominates the higher groups late in the flow. Removing either term with the trunk fixed raises velocity MSE: at t=0.90 by 32.1 (spatial) or 64.1 (spectral), and at t=0.05 by 1.1 and 2.1. The spectral branch is the main scaffold throughout these probes; the spatial branch supplies an additional late, higher-frequency correction under this parameterization.

sections.title: 7 Conclusion
sections.content: SpecSlot recasts tokenization as allocation: fixed token budget is split between anchor density and spectral subdivision, while global attention is assigned by role. On ImageNet-256, it reaches comparable final FID to the FLOPs-matched JiT control and descends faster early in training; on ImageNet-512, it improves FID by 2.84 over that control and approaches JiT-B/16 at 38% lower cost. On text-to-image generation, the same design surpasses JiT-B/8 on DPG-Bench (62.21 vs. 61.15) at 40.6% lower forward cost. These results show that, in the evaluated pixel-space settings, output detail and global-communication cost can be decoupled through tokenization. Our diagnostics find the lowest-radial role is recovered earliest, supporting its use as the carrier. Allocation gives pixel-space models new way to trade detail for communication.

sections.title: E Additional Mechanistic Diagnostics
sections.content: This appendix collects measurements that probe how SpecSlot uses its explicit roles. Unless stated otherwise, probe loads checkpoint and intervenes on its states without updating any parameter; these results characterize representation and communication rather than claim end-to-end quality gains. For the route probe, the intervention is made inside the shared Transformer after slot formation and before the output head, so its interpretation concerns the spectral-slot/GGLL submodule rather than particular output basis. E.1 Evidence timing and route interventions We first measure an empirical data-to-noise ratio (DNR) for each radial coefficient group in the lapped frame. For group k, DNRk(t) = t2EAkx2/[(1 t)2EAkϵ2], where Ak denotes the matched lapped-frame analysis restricted to that group. The crossing time is the first flow time at which the group reaches DNR 1; it is 18 Table 14 Empirical DNR frontiers from the lapped-frame probe. Entries list the crossing times in increasing radial-group order. Allocation for successive radial groups 256/K8 256/K4 1024/K2 {0.549, 0.936} {0.382, 0.836, 0.880, 0.904, 0.922, 0.933, 0.943, 0.959} {0.468, 0.891, 0.928, 0.951} descriptive measure of when the noisy input contains more signal than noise, not learned gate. Table 14 reports the crossings for the paired W256/K8, W256/K4, and W1024/K2 checkpoints. The frontiers move when or changes: the low group becomes usable earlier, while progressively finer groups become usable later. This is consistent with assigning the early cross-anchor path to the lowest radial role. In the matched teacher-forced route intervention, removing the global carrier path primarily increases the low-group and early error; removing local mixing primarily increases detail-group error later in the trajectory. For example, the mid-time log-MSE penalties for the W256/K8 and W256/K4 probes are approximately 0.14/1.66 and 0.20/2.14 (global/local). The on-policy intervention has the same ordering: global removal changes the early coarse field (low-frequency change about 0.98, 0.99, and 1.05 for the three allocations), while local removal continues to change mid/high frequency content in the middle and late segments. These measurements are consistent with the role assignment used by GGLL. E.2 Allocation and effective use of additional slots To separate single-step fitting from the use of extra role slots, paired fixed-W = 256, fixed-B = 1536 analysis compares {2, 4, 8}. The models share the input, lapped output, and GGLL interfaces used by the registered K-rate diagnostic. For reproducibility, the effective-slot value is the entropy effective rank of each anchors slot Gram matrix, divided by K; the effective-local-key value is exp(Hq)/K averaged over local queries, with Hq = (cid:80) pqj log pqj; and detail-to-carrier is the mean local attention probability from detail queries to the carrier key. Table 5 in Section 5.1.1 shows that although the teacher-forced velocity error changes little, the fraction of effective slots and the fraction of local keys decline as the within-anchor sequence grows. Thus adding slots can slightly improve teacher-forced fitting without providing the same number of independent, strongly coupled directions. This is consistent with an allocation sweet spot: controls how finely the coefficient ownership is divided, but it is not promise that every added slot contributes an equal amount of information.

sections.title: F Paired Qualitative Comparisons
sections.content: F.1 ImageNet examples Figure 9 compares selected ImageNet-256 generations from JiT-CM and SpecSlot W256/K4 under the same class and noise draw. In these pairs, SpecSlot renders class-specific fine structure more coherently: feather boundaries are clearer for brambling, chickadee, and rooster; the cornet has more regular tubing and bell geometry; and the boathouse preserves sharper roofline and reflection structure. It also reduces visible local distortions in the anemone fish, banister, and barrel examples, where contours or repeated parts are less coherent in the JiT-CM samples. The hay example shows more regular field-scale texture. F.2 Text-to-image examples Figure 10 shows additional SpecSlot samples generated from text prompts in DPG-Bench. The examples cover portraits, creatures, environments, architecture, and interiors; the prompt paired with each sample is included in the figure. 19 Figure 9 Selected paired generations on ImageNet-256.
